original_value: Estimating the effects of an intervention from high-dimensional observational data is a challenging problem due to the existence of confounding. The task is often further complicated in healthcare applications where a set of observations may be entirely missing for certain patients at test time, thereby prohibiting accurate inference. In this paper, we address this issue using an approach based on the information bottleneck to reason about the effects of interventions. To this end, we first train an information bottleneck to perform a low-dimensional compression of covariates by explicitly considering the relevance of information for treatment effects. As a second step, we subsequently use the compressed covariates to perform a transfer of relevant information to cases where data are missing during testing. In doing so, we can reliably and accurately estimate treatment effects even in the absence of a full set of covariate information at test time. Our results on two causal inference benchmarks and a real application for treating sepsis show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, without compromising interpretability.

result.paraphrase: Estimating intervention effects from high-dimensional observational data is difficult because of confounding. In healthcare settings, the problem is often made harder when some patients have entirely missing observations at test time, which prevents accurate inference. This paper tackles the issue with an information-bottleneck-based approach for reasoning about intervention effects. First, we train an information bottleneck to compress covariates into a low-dimensional representation while explicitly accounting for which information is relevant to treatment effects. Next, we use the compressed covariates to transfer relevant information to test cases with missing data. This allows reliable, accurate estimation of treatment effects even when a complete set of covariates is unavailable at test time. Results on two causal inference benchmarks and a real sepsis treatment application show state-of-the-art performance without sacrificing interpretability.
